analysis.one_liner: Bans natural gas price gouging by utilities in federally declared disaster areas.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for a utility company to charge unconscionably excessive prices for natural gas — wholesale or retail — in any county covered by a federally declared major disaster, and for a year afterward. The Federal Trade Commission, working with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, would decide when a price crosses the line. Violating companies could face civil penalties up to $100 million (or triple their illegal profits), criminal fines up to $500 million, and lawsuits from state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that buy natural gas in counties covered by a federal major disaster declaration. The bill would give the FTC and FERC a federal standard for judging gas prices as unconscionably excessive, let the FTC prioritize companies with more than $2 billion a year in gas sales, and let state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents for retail price gouging. It would not preempt stronger state laws.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any gas utility to charge a price the FTC, working with FERC, finds unconscionably excessive and exploitative of a major disaster, covering both wholesale and retail sales in any county under the declaration and for one year after it ends [S3].

Puts real teeth behind the ban: civil penalties of up to three times the illegal profits or $100 million, criminal fines up to $500 million prosecuted by the Attorney General, each day of a continuing violation counted separately, and priority enforcement against utilities with over $2 billion in annual gas sales [S3].
Lets state attorneys general sue in federal court on behalf of their residents over retail price gouging, while leaving state anti-gouging laws fully intact [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas utility companies, which would face federal price-gouging exposure with penalties up to $100 million civil and $500 million criminal during and after major disasters. To the extent the rules make utilities more cautious about pricing during supply disruptions, some of that caution could show up in rates reviewed by regulators, borne by ratepayers.

drawbacks.text: The standard is vague: 'unconscionably excessive' with 'unfair advantage' is left to FTC determination, so utilities would face large penalties for conduct whose legality depends on a regulator's judgment call rather than a bright line [S3].

Natural gas prices legitimately spike when disasters disrupt supply, and a rule that treats disaster-period increases as evidence of gouging could deter utilities from passing through genuine cost increases or discourage suppliers from serving disaster areas at all [S3].

The penalty structure is unusually harsh — a criminal fine of up to $500 million on top of civil penalties for what is fundamentally a pricing violation, without any showing of fraud or physical harm [S3].

Many states, including California, already have price-gouging laws, so the bill adds a federal enforcement layer on top of existing state protections, with a provision that pauses state suits against a defendant once the FTC or FERC sues [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is real but modest in scope: it only applies during and shortly after federally declared disasters, and it targets a specific pricing practice rather than utility rates generally. The main cost is uncertainty for utilities facing severe penalties under a loosely defined standard, which honest supporters would acknowledge; the bill tries to soften this by requiring courts to weigh the seriousness of the violation and the company's remediation efforts. On balance it is a targeted consumer protection with an unusually aggressive penalty scheme.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Josh Harder introduced the bill on April 13, 2023, with no cosponsors [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on April 21, 2023 to its Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large gas utilities, PG&E foremost among them, are better off because the bill died: they face no new federal price-gouging penalties during disasters. Gas customers in disaster areas gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gas utilities that avoided new penalties

for.name: Rep. Josh Harder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress; it never drew a cosponsor

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee and its Energy, Climate and Grid Security subcommittee for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee calendar and never scheduled the bill for consideration

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for any vote; its only sponsor was a Democrat and it attracted zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would expose large gas utilities to federal price-gouging penalties of up to $100 million civil and $500 million criminal whenever they raise gas prices in a disaster-declared county. Because the bill died, they avoided that exposure entirely; PG&E, the bill's namesake target, faces no new federal gouging liability.

industries.industry: Gas wholesalers and marketers selling to utilities
industries.note: The prohibition covers wholesale as well as retail sales, so upstream sellers could not charge disaster-inflated prices to utilities either. They are spared the same exposure because the bill died.
